class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Some worry Flock cameras, like this one on the UIC campus, could be used to identify and discipline students and faculty if they attend a protest or express opinions universities and the federal government find problematic.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Some students and faculty say the use of Flock equipment to surveil American campuses is especially troubling because universities are meant to be places where people can discuss and study ideas freely. They worry Flock cameras could be used to identify and discipline students and faculty <a class="Link" href="https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2025/11/how-cops-are-using-flock-safetys-alpr-network-surveil-protesters-and-activists?ref=404media.co" target="_blank" ><u>if they attend a protest</u></a> or express opinions universities and the federal government find problematic.</p><p>People worry “they will be singled out, they could face repercussions, and all of that is really, in my mind, antithetical to the ideals of the university,” said Torin Monahan, a surveillance researcher at the University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill.</p><p>The presence of Flock cameras adds another layer of concern at schools like UIC that pride themselves on supporting underrepresented and marginalized students, because the data collected can endanger immigrant and international students and students of color.</p><p>Last year, <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilsos.gov/news/2025/august-25-2025-giannoulias-audit-finds-license-plate-reader-company-in-violation-of-state-law.html" target="_blank" ><u>an audit by the Illinois secretary of state</u></a> found that U.S. Customs and Border Protection had searched Flock databases across Illinois in violation of the state’s Trust Act, which bans cooperation between Illinois law enforcement and federal immigration authorities. Earlier in 2025, <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/abortion-access-immigration-license-plate-readers-surveillance-13fac7c045df3c5e5145f6d4e4c4db28" target="_blank" ><u>the same state office</u></a> found that Texas agents searched Flock databases in Illinois to pursue a woman who had an abortion.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-2f0000" name="html-embed-module-2f0000"></a><div style="min-height:828px" id="datawrapper-vis-tYxZn"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/tYxZn/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-tYxZn"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/tYxZn/full.png" alt="Five public universities contract with Flock Safety in Illinois (Symbol map)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Flock claims the company has <a class="Link" href="https://www.flocksafety.com/blog/flock-guardrails-address-lpr-privacy-concerns-and-police-transparency" target="_blank" ><u>made changes</u></a> in the last year that allow police forces to limit who can access camera data. But as of this summer, outside agencies were still frequently searching the data collected at some Illinois public colleges.</p><p>In early August, WBEZ filed a public records request for a log of external agencies that had searched Flock data from the University of Illinois System since early 2025 and for what reasons.</p><p>System officials said the request was too burdensome because it turned up such a large volume of data — and revealed that outside law enforcement had searched Flock data from the three campuses more than 650,000 times over a 30-day period in July and August.</p><p>“The police I've been interviewing will say that they want to protect the campus community,” Monahan said. </p><p>But he questioned if university administrators want to be embracing this “fortress mentality” given the many trade-offs. “Do they want to be on the wrong side of these privacy concerns and these surveillance risks to their populations?”</p><h3>‘Why are we gathering this giant pool of information?’</h3><p>Among Illinois public universities, the University of Illinois System is Flock’s biggest client.</p><p>UIC has a two-year, $110,300 <a class="Link" href="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/19/43/adaa6cdf4158a9edcceeef346b14/flock-on-campus-contracts-unis.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>contract with Flock</u></a> to operate 15 cameras on university property, according to documents obtained through public records requests.</p><p>UIC leaders denied a request for an interview. But spokesperson Sherri McGinnis Gonzalez said via email that Flock’s surveillance technology enables “investigators to identify vehicles associated with reported crimes, public safety threats and Amber Alerts.”</p><p>She said the university’s contract ends this month, but officials are in talks to renew it.</p><p>“The safety of our students, faculty, staff, patients and visitors is a top priority,” McGinnis Gonzalez wrote. “UIC is committed to transparency, accountability and privacy protections in its use of public safety technology.”</p><p>In addition to its contract with Flock, UIC officials agreed in December 2025 to pay a <a class="Link" href="https://volt.ai/the-future-of-campus-security-how-the-university-of-illinois-chicago-secures-a-diverse-urban-campus-with-volt-ai" target="_blank" ><u>company called Volt Inc.</u></a> $3.5 million over three years for AI-powered video detection of weapons, “crowd formation” and “unattended objects,” public records show.</p><p>A university spokesperson said via email that campus police hired Volt “to detect potential security issues in real time and quickly alert UIC Police, helping improve campus safety,” adding that the Flock and Volt systems operate separately.</p><p>Flock signed the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign as its first public university client in the state in 2021, records show. A university spokesperson said the campus has since paid more than $180,000 to the company.</p><p>Leaders there denied an interview request. But in a written statement, a spokesperson said their Flock surveillance network of 20 cameras had “recently proved integral in investigations involving sexual assault, robbery, suicidal or missing persons, aggravated battery, and stolen vehicles, just to name a few.”</p><p>SIU Carbondale officials denied a request for an interview and refused to answer questions over email.</p><p>In all, more than 150,000 students at Illinois public universities are subject to surveillance on their campuses by Flock’s AI-powered tech, whether they are driving to class or getting dropped off in their family car on move-in day. That's in addition to the many faculty, visitors and others who drive by campus daily.</p><p>Monahan said he worries not only about student privacy, but also about data security. Flock claims that local agencies own the data from their cameras, but that data is housed on Flock-owned servers, Monahan said, and used to train Flock’s AI models.</p><p>“What are you learning about the people on a campus through these systems that can then be fed into these artificial intelligence systems and monetized by a third party, such as Flock?” Monahan asked.</p><div class="Enhancement" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>UIC students Rachel Stein (left) and Ellie Prafcke have walked by this Flock camera on UIC’s campus many times, but didn’t know it was an AI-powered surveillance camera until a WBEZ reporter told them.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Lisa Kurian Philip/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Some students have similar concerns.</p><p>“Why are we gathering this giant pool of information just in case it might help if somebody's car might get stolen and drive on this road?” said Ellie Prafcke, a visiting student at UIC. “I feel like there are many other ways that we can solve crimes rather than just taking in random data.”</p><p>Prafcke and her friend Rachel Stein said they hope UIC leaders will take the time to get feedback from students before they sign off on a new contract with Flock. The two even have an idea for how to go about doing so.</p><p>“Set up a sign right here,” Stein said, pointing to a camera in front of UIC’s computer design building. Tell students: “This is a Flock camera. This is what it does. Here's a QR code to tell us your opinion about whether you want this here or not.”</p><p>“Then before you sign the contract,” Stein said, “think about what the students want.”</p><p><i>Lisa Kurian Philip covers higher education for WBEZ in partnership with</i> <a class="Link" href="https://www.opencampusmedia.org/" target="_blank" ><i>Open Campus</i></a><i>.</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/flock-license-plate-reader-explainer" >What to know about Flock’s controversial license plate readers</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/27/flock-license-plate-reader-alpr-chicago-suburb" >Flock license plate readers turn Chicago suburbs into ground zero for bitter fight over surveillance</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/09/01/illinois-cities-halt-flock-use-suspend-officers-and-review-policy-amid-alleged-improper-use" >Illinois suburbs halt Flock use, suspend officers and review policy amid alleged improper use</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Oprah Winfrey returns with an 'immersive' live show at the Sphere in Las Vegas
entries.summary: <p>Fifteen years after ending “<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/movies-and-tv/2024/11/27/oprah-wildest-dreams-winfrey-car-pontiac-g6-paolo-presta" >The Oprah Winfrey Show</a>” in Chicago, the media mogul is returning to deliver more engaging conversations and “aha” moments in front of an audience outside of the Midwest.</p><p>She will bring “Oprah Winfrey’s AHA” to Sphere in Las Vegas April 2-4, 2027. The venture is not a televised talk show but an “immersive” live experience, featuring music, storytelling and more, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.sphereentertainmentco.com/oprah-winfreys-aha-a-first-of-its-kind-immersive-experience-debuts-live-at-sphere-for-one-weekend-april-2-4-2027/" target="_blank" >an announcement</a> on Sphere’s website. The two-hour event promises a unique presentation of light and sound, taking advantage of the venue’s globe-shaped space, 580,000-square-foot LED exterior, and the 160,000-square-foot, wraparound LED display inside.</p><p>Special guests include singer-songwriter Jacob Collier, poet and author Ocean Vuong, musician Ajeet and gospel singer Wintley Phipps.</p><p>“‘AHA’ is a dream that came to me as I sat in awe at the opening night of U2 at the Sphere, mesmerized by the possibilities of how the space could be used as a tool for creating greater awareness and understanding of ourselves and our connection to each other,” Winfrey said in a release.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/UuFiWC0uIac?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Introducing Oprah Winfrey's AHA"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>The show’s musical direction will be guided by composer Max Richter, musician and vocal director Jason White, and electronic artist and producer Jon Hopkins. Oscar-winning “Moonlight” screenwriter <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/theater/2026/04/10/windfall-steppenwolf-play-tarell-alvin-mccraney-moonlight-writer" >Tarell Alvin McCraney</a>, who has premiered work at Chicago's Steppenwolf, will help write the show, while artist Es Devlin and the Plum Village Monks will contribute original works.</p><p>Tickets start at $145 and go on sale Sept. 25 at 10 a.m. Pacific Time. Prospective attendees can sign up for a presale and view travel packages at <a class="Link" href="http://ahalive.com" target="_blank" ><u>AHAlive.com</u></a>.</p><p>Oprah began her career in Chicago in 1984 on WLS-TV’s morning talk show, “A.M. Chicago.” It was renamed “The Oprah Winfrey Show” in 1985 and taped at <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2015/3/3/18575251/oprah-s-harpo-studios-to-close-in-december" >Harpo Studios</a> on the Near West Side from 1990 to 2011.</p>
entries.author: Erica Thompson

entries.title: Morning storms blamed for nearly 1,000 delays at Chicago airports
entries.summary: <p>Early morning thunderstorms caused ground stops at O'Hare and Midway airports and one to three inches of rain fell throughout the Chicago area in "the most rain we've seen in a month," according to forecasters. </p><p>Roughly three inches of rain fell in Aurora and two inches of rain was reported in Romeoville, according to the National Weather Service. About seven-tenths-of-an-inch fell at O'Hare and Midway saw 1.6 inches of rain. </p><p>Ground stops were initially reported at both airports early Thursday morning but flights are moving with an average delay of over two hours, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. </p><p>As of 9:25 a.m., 159 flights were canceled at O'Hare with over 800 more facing delays, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.flightaware.com/live/cancelled/today/ord" target="_blank" >FlightAware</a>. At Midway, over 25 flights were canceled while over 135 more were delayed. </p><p>A flood advisory was in effect for the Chicago metro area until 10:30 a.m., though meteorologist Brett Borchardt says the heaviest rain of the day is behind us. </p><p>"We are still going to have some spotty showers and storms through the next few hours across the morning, but otherwise we are looking at a largely dry rest of the day," Borchardt said. </p><p>Borchardt urges commuters to be mindful of slippery road conditions related to Thursday morning's storms. </p><p>"If [you] do come upon an intersection or road that is flooded over, [you] just never want to drive through that since we don't know how deep it is," Borchardt said. </p><p>The Chicago area will get a slight stretch of dry conditions before rainfall returns Friday night into early Saturday. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Man mauled by dog in Edgewater
entries.summary: <p>A man was seriously injured after a dog-walker attacked him and ordered his dog to bite him early Wednesday in Edgewater.</p><p>The 44-year-old man was outside in the 5900 block of North Sheridan Road around 3 a.m. Wednesday when the dog-walker approached him and began yelling at him, Chicago police said. </p><p>The man walked away when the dog-walker struck him in the head and face and ordered his dog to bite him, police said. </p><p>He suffered cuts and animal bites and relocated to the 1100 block of West Thorndale Avenue before he was taken to St. Francis Hospital in Evanston in serious condition, officials said. </p><p>Area 3 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Illinois residents who are terminally ill can now end their lives. Here’s how it works.
entries.summary: <p>In Illinois, terminally ill residents with less than six months to live can now request a prescription for medication to end their lives.</p><p>Illinois <a class="Link" href="https://www.aadm.org/courses/state-map-and-state-aid-in-dying-laws" target="_blank" ><u>joins 12 other states</u></a> and Washington D.C., in legalizing medical aid in dying. In Illinois, it’s called “Deb’s Law,” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024/2/9/24066104/illinois-right-to-die-legislation-general-assembly" target="_blank" ><u>inspired by Deb Robertson</u></a>, a former social worker in suburban Lombard who has an aggressive form of cancer. Robertson spent years advocating for the right to end her life with medication, should she choose to do so.</p><p>After much <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024/2/9/24066104/illinois-right-to-die-legislation-general-assembly" target="_blank" ><u>emotional debate</u></a>, Illinois lawmakers ultimately passed the proposed bill with 30 yays and 27 nays. Gov. JB Pritzker <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/12/12/illinois-right-to-die-pritzker-signs-law" target="_blank" ><u>signed it into law</u></a> on Dec. 12, 2025, recalling how he’d been moved by stories of people in Illinois or their loved ones who suffered from a terminal illness.</p><p>But the measure has become <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/09/03/cardinal-blase-cupich-chicago-archdiocese-nuns-challenge-right-to-die-law-assisted-suicide" target="_blank" ><u>a lightning rod</u></a> for some religious and disability rights groups who worry it could lead to abuse. Despite court challenges, the law still stands.</p><p>Here’s what to know about medical aid in dying in Illinois.</p><p><b>How does Deb’s Law work?</b></p><p>Using a <a class="Link" href="https://dph.illinois.gov/content/dam/soi/en/web/idph/forms/topics-services/provider-partner-resources/end-of-life-options-for-terminally-ill/eol-options-for-terminally-ill-act-request.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>new state form</u></a>, a patient makes a written request to their doctor to get a prescription for medication that would end their life. They also must make two verbal requests at least five days apart, <a class="Link" href="https://dph.illinois.gov/topics-services/provider-partner-resources/end-of-life-options-for-terminally-ill/information-for-patients.html#forms" target="_blank" ><u>according to the state</u></a>. Patients could hand their doctor a letter and make their first verbal request at the same time. A second physician must approve the request.</p><p>Physicians can waive the waiting period for patients who are expected to die within five days.</p><p>Patients must be able to swallow medication on their own or through a feeding tube. It’s typically a mixture of several drugs specially prepared into a powder that can be mixed into water or juice.</p><p>Doctors must tell patients about potential risks, and likely outcome if they take the medication, that they can rescind their request, and that they don’t have to take the medication.</p><p>Physicians who have concerns about a patient’s mental capacity would refer them to a mental health provider who could halt the process.</p><p>Patients would get their prescription filled through a specialty pharmacy that prepares customized medications.</p><p><b>How do you find a doctor who is participating?</b></p><p>Patients largely have to navigate this on their own. There is no directory of doctors or pharmacies in Illinois offering medical aid in dying. <a class="Link" href="https://ilga.gov/Legislation/ILCS/Articles?ActID=4646&ChapterID=35&Chapter=PUBLIC%20HEALTH&MajorTopic=HEALTH%20AND%20SAFETY&Print=True" target="_blank" ><u>Doctors are not required</u></a> to participate, but they must help patients get a referral to a physician who would say yes. (Doctors are shielded from prosecution whether they participate or refuse to).</p><p>A lack of guidance from the state, which has had about nine months to prepare for the law to take effect, is frustrating people who work with patients who are dying. Some patients in hospice care are already asking about the new law, and there’s no physician or pharmacy to refer them to, said Sara Dado, executive director of the Illinois Hospice and Palliative Care Organization. The advocacy group has about 35 members across the state, from small hospice centers to ones that are part of big hospitals.</p><p>The majority of her members don’t plan to write prescriptions for medication to end someone's life. But many would refer patients to a doctor who would. Hospitals have told Dado they’re still figuring out if and how they plan to participate, while several religiously-affiliated medical centers have already opted out.</p><p>This is par for the course. Doctors took a wait and see approach in other states that rolled out medical aid in dying, said Thalia DeWolf, associate director of education for the Academy of Aid-in-Dying Medicine. The nonprofit trains doctors to doulas across the U.S. on end of life care and does not advocate for or against medical aid in dying.</p><p>A spokeswoman for the Illinois Department of Public Health declined an interview but answered questions over email. She said the state has sent “communications” to health care providers about the law and plans to hold a webinar.</p><p><b>What are potential barriers for patients? </b></p><p>There are no requirements in Deb’s Law that insurers must cover the cost of medication, and they typically don’t.</p><p>The lack of insurance coverage could be a big hurdle for people who can least afford to pay, DeWolf said. The medication in some states ranges from $600 to $1,000 out of pocket.</p><p>Finding a physician who speaks your language or having access to interpreters can also be a challenge.</p><p><b>Is there opposition to the law? </b></p><p>Yes. There is still some opposition, including <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/09/03/cardinal-blase-cupich-chicago-archdiocese-nuns-challenge-right-to-die-law-assisted-suicide" target="_blank" ><u>from Cardinal Blase Cupich</u></a> in Chicago, who is part of a federal lawsuit that alleges medical aid in dying is unconstitutional and denies “the choice of a dignified death” to Catholics who want to die naturally.</p><p>In the past roughly 30 years since Oregon voters passed the first medical aid in dying law in the U.S., <a class="Link" href="https://compassionandchoices.org/resource/medical-aid-in-dying-utilization-report/" target="_blank" ><u>more than 20,000 people</u></a> in places where medical aid in dying is legal received prescriptions, with at least 12,000 ingesting medication, according to Compassion and Choices, a national nonprofit that advocated for medical aid in dying in Illinois.</p><p><i>Contributing: Jon Seidel </i></p><p><i>Kristen Schorsch is a senior reporter covering public health for WBEZ.</i></p>

>Illinois universities use Flock cams to surveil campus: records</a></h3><h3></h3><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydyhudyd-l-h/" target="_blank" >Lisa Kurian Philip</a></h5><p><b>Flock U</b>: As cities and colleges in Illinois and across the country cut ties with Flock Safety, a WBEZ review of contracts found that five of the state's 12 public universities still work with the controversial surveillance tech company. The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, the University of Illinois Chicago, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, Western Illinois University and the University of Illinois Springfield have together spent more than $450,000 on Flock's services since 2021, records show.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: Flock's automatic license plate readers <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydyhudyd-l-k/" target="_blank" >use cameras and artificial intelligence</a> to capture data about every passing vehicle, including plate numbers, make and model, dents and bumper stickers. That information is logged onto a database searchable by campus police and outside law enforcement.</p><p><b>The controversy</b>: College leaders say the surveillance helps solve crimes and keep campuses and students safe. But Flock has come under public scrutiny following revelations that police officers have used the company's cameras to stalk their exes. Data captured by Flock cameras have also led to wrongful arrests. At universities like UIC and Western Illinois University, students have started petitioning their schools to stop working with the company.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydyhudyd-l-u/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>HEALTH AND HOUSING ✶</h4><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-520000" name="image-520000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4af60af/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb2%2F67%2F1366b2214391ae6163af397fa2c3%2Fcoolingviolation-260911-5.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d32666f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb2%2F67%2F1366b2214391ae6163af397fa2c3%2Fcoolingviolation-260911-5.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3458c3e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb2%2F67%2F1366b2214391ae6163af397fa2c3%2Fcoolingviolation-260911-5.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="The building at 6565 S. Yale Ave., became the first to violate the city's cooling ordinance this year when its chiller broke in late August. Records show the failed inspection occurred Aug. 31. The first hearing in the case was Sept. 2. Under the ordinance, landlords and building owners can be fined up to $1,000 per day, per violation.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: Chicago's cooling ordinance was established after the heat-related deaths of three elderly women at the James Sneider Apartments in Rogers Park in 2022. The ordinance requires certain buildings — including nursing homes, housing for older persons, high-rises above 80 feet, and residential buildings with 100 or more units — to provide air conditioning class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydyhudyd-l-th/" target="_blank" >Courtney Kueppers</a></h5><p>Chicago has had an especially big year for jazz, beginning when the city hosted the UNESCO International Jazz Day in April. But local fans know September is the city's true jazz month, with free festivals across town.</p><p>From Thursday through Sunday, the 27th annual <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydyhudyd-l-tk/" target="_blank" >Englewood Jazz Festival</a>, founded by saxophonist Ernest Dawkins, will feature up-and-coming musicians, including members of the longstanding training ensemble, the Young Masters. The event will also celebrate all-time greats like John Coltrane, born 100 years ago.</p><p>Then, Sept. 26 and 27, the multi-venue <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydyhudyd-l-tu/" target="_blank" >Hyde Park Jazz Festival</a> will ring in its 20th year.</p><p>We've rounded up 10 sets you won't want to miss at these South Side festivals.</p><p>Our picks include: The Julius Tucker Trio and the Live the Spirit Residency Expanded Ensemble (Englewood Jazz Festival); plus, Orbert Davis' sextet and a jazz fest anniversary band featuring trumpeter Marquis Hill, drummer Makaya McCraven, bassist Junius Paul and vibraphonist Joel Ross (Hyde Park Jazz Festival).</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydyhudyd-l-il/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p>Both of Chicago's airports <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydyhudyd-l-ir/" target="_blank" >have again been ranked below average in JD Power’s airport customer satisfaction survey</a>, with O'Hare tying for last in "mega airports" with New Jersey's Newark Liberty Airport. So we want to know: <b><u>What would you change or improve about Chicago's airports?</u> Be sure to tell us which airport you're talking about.</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Reply to this question via email</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). We may run your answer in a future newsletter or story.</i></p><p>Yesterday, we asked you: <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydyhudyd-l-iy/" target="_blank" >How do you feel about City Council’s potential new parking meter deal?</a></p><p>Here’s some of what you said, edited for length and clarity:</p><p>"It seems like keeping the rates reasonable should be part of the deal.  And I'd much prefer that the city buy the contract and get the meters back under its control." — <i>Glenn Burkhardt</i></p><p>"I'm tired of deals the city makes. Their shortsightedness always makes them losers in the short and long run." — <i>Donald Smith</i></p><p>"I’m really impressed with the gains made by the city council team. Actually, I’m shocked! Could it be that government can be functional? The original deal has been an albatross. ... The fact that city council members got together to negotiate a decent outcome is to be applauded." — <i>Kathleen Alaimo</i></p><p>"It's great that the old parking deal is evolving, but it's difficult to square 'lucrative benefits for the city and motorists' with important city goals to improve living conditions and reduce costs by moving away from private car travel." — <i>Melanie Eckner</i></p><hr><p>Thanks for reading the Sun-Times Morning Edition!<br>Got a story you think we missed? <a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >Email us here.</a></p><hr><p><b>Written and curated by</b>: Matt Moore<br><b>Editor</b>: Michael Lansu</p>

entries.title: Boy, 13, critically injured in beating near Gately Park in Roseland
entries.summary: <p>Detectives were speaking with a witness and trying to find video evidence after a 13-year-old boy was beaten and critically wounded Saturday in Roseland near Gately Park on the Far South Side. </p><p>Calumet District police officers responded to a call of a battery in progress about noon on Saturday in the 10200 block of South Cottage Grove Avenue. </p><p>There, they found the 13-year-old boy unresponsive and a witness told them he'd been beaten by four people only described as males who "continued to batter him after he lost consciousness," according to a Chicago police report obtained by the Sun-Times.</p><p>The boy, who suffered "blunt force trauma to the head," was taken to Comer Children’s Hospital in critical condition, according to the report. </p><p>Area 2 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: CATCH 22: Week 1 fireworks wow former Bears advisor Bill Polian
entries.summary: <p>Analyzing at the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> with the help of 22 names, starting with …</p><p><b>Bill Polian (1), </b>the former general manager of the Bills, Colts and expansion Panthers. The last time I’d spoken to him, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2022/2/9/22926406/bears-coach-gm-search-bill-polian-quarterback-justin-fields-not-blue-chipper-yet-give-chance-grow" target="_blank" >Polian</a> had just finished evaluating the Bears’ 2021 roster for his friend <b>George McCaskey</b> (<b>2)</b>, who then fired general manager <b>Ryan Pace (3)</b> and hired <b>Ryan Poles (4)</b>. Polian polled personnel people inside and outside Halas Hall and decided the team had six players —maybe eight, if he was feeling generous— with whom the Bears could win consistently.</p><p>“The rest,” he told me in February 2022, “were either questionable or not good.”</p><p>Polian, who lives in suburban Charlotte, went to Sunday’s 59-37 fireworks display. The Pro Football Hall of Famer was justifiably impressed.</p><p>“Ryan’s done a great job of building a team with solid contributors — and getting play-makers on top of that,” he said. “The coach has taken it to another level.”</p><p>He guessed the Bears had three times as many impact players as four-and-a-half years ago, naming receiver <b>Rome Odunze</b> <b>(5)</b> and tight ends <b>Colston Loveland (6)</b> and <b>Cole Kmet (7)</b>. He saved his most praise for <b>Caleb Williams (8)</b>.</p><p>“The quarterback is incredible, really,” said Polian, turns 84 in December. “His talent level is almost off the charts. Some of the throws that he makes and the fact he was so accurate, especially when he was outside the pocket. The acceleration he has when he runs with the ball, I imagine if you’ve not played him before, as was the case with the Panthers, you’re astounded at his speed. Their commitment to the running game is just marvelous. And it’s the perfect match with the quarterback’s skillset. …</p><p>“They’re a really fun team to watch. That’s exciting football, to say the least.”</p><p>He has faith that defensive coordinator <b>Dennis Allen (9) </b>will shore up the defense. If they do, the Bears’ ceiling is the roof, to quote another Carolinian, <b>Michael Jordan (10)</b>.</p><p>Polian credited the GM for having the right sense of what his team needed and the confidence to trade the 2023 No. 1 overall pick to the Panthers. The trade stocked the Bears roster to the point it’s almost unrecognizable from 2022.</p><p>“They’re absolutely on the right track, no question about it,” Polian said. “They play the right way to win, both in Chicago and in the long run.”</p><h3><b>The most disappointing performance Sunday came from …</b></h3><h3></h3><p><b>Jaylon Johnson (11), </b>who allowed a 113.7 passer rating on balls thrown in his direction.</p><p>“I wasn’t into it how I needed to be, mentally or physically,” Johnson said Wednesday, “and I think it just trickled throughout the defense.”</p><p>That’s a disturbing development for a Bears defense that desperately needs Johnson to stay healthy and effective. Johnson needs it too — he considers this season to be a walk year and a chance to make big money on his next deal.</p><p>Healthy for the first time since 2024, Johnson did make one game-changing play, forcing a fumble on the first play of the fourth quarter. But his performance was so bad that defensive backs coach <b>Al Harris (12) </b>playfully demurred Thursday when asked to evaluate Johnson’s tape. Both Johnson and <b>Tyrique Stevenson (13)</b>, who gave up a perfect 158.3 passer rating, were justifiably upset about their Week 1 performances, Harris said.</p><p>It only gets harder this week, when Johnsonfaces the Vikings’ <b>Justin Jefferson (14), </b>whom he considers one of the best two receivers in football.</p><p>“I don’t think there’s a flaw to his game,” the cornerback said.<br>That evaluation is by reputation more than personal experience, though. This will be the 13<sup>th</sup> game the Vikings and Bears have played each other since Jefferson and Johnson came into the league together in 2020. Amazingly, the two have been on the field at the same time in only four games. Johnson missed both meetings last season with a groin injury.</p><h3><b>The last QB to beat the Vikings at Soldier Field was …</b></h3><p><b>Chase Daniel (15), </b>who took when <b>Mitch Trubisky</b> <b>(16)</b> when he hurt his left shoulder after a first-quarter sack in 2019. The Bears have beaten 17 different franchises at Soldier Field since — including the Giants a whopping four times.</p><p><b>The Vikings have started 9 different QBs since 2023, most recently …</b></p><p><b>Kyler Murray (17), </b>who was concussed in<b> </b>Sunday’s<b> </b>opener. The Bears have started three during that same time: Williams, <b>Justin Fields (18)</b> and <b>Tyson Bagent (19).</b></p><h3><b>And since this whole column is about names …</b></h3><p><b>Beggs Gardner (20</b>), the Bears’ rookie long snapper, became the first Beggs to ever play an NFL game when he made his debut Sunday. Gardner has gone by his nickname Beau his whole life, though, and that’s what he’s called on the roster. He was named after a great uncle, <b>John Irvin Beggs</b> <b>(21)</b>, a titan of the early electric industry who was a lifelong friend of <b>Thomas Edison (22)</b> and the one-time director of his company. He left inheritance to descendants who, among other things, imported the London Bridge to Lake Havasu City, Arizona.</p><p>“Interesting fella,” Gardner said.</p>

entries.title: Man's body found in police vehicle at Far South Side station
entries.summary: <p>Foul play is not suspected after the body of a man was found in a parked police vehicle at the city's Calumet District station in the Pullman neighborhood on the Far South Side.</p><p>The remains were found in the backseat of a new, unused police vehicle while vehicles were being moved around at about 9:15 a.m. in the 700 block of East 112th Street, police said.</p><p>The vehicle has never been in service and was parked at the East 112th Street address. The victim, whose name and age were not immediately known, was dead on the scene.</p><p>No foul play is suspected, according to police, who said the remains may have been there for a while. </p><p>Area 2 detectives are conducting a death investigation.<br></p>

entries.title: Pope Leo XIV appoints new bishop of the Diocese of Joliet
entries.summary: <p>Pope Leo XIV has appointed a new bishop of the Diocese of Joliet. </p><p>Bishop Brendan J. Cahill will serve as the seventh bishop of the Diocese of Joliet. Cahill has served as bishop of the Diocese of Victoria, Texas, since his appointment by Pope Francis in 2015, the diocese said. His installation Mass will be scheduled for November 2026.</p><p>The Diocese of Joliet serves approximately 500,000 Catholics in DuPage, Ford, Grundy, Iroquois, Kankakee, Kendall and Will counties, making it the second largest arm of the Catholic Church in the Chicago area.</p><p>Ronald Hicks, the former bishop of the Diocese of Joliet, was appointed by Pope Leo as the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/religion/2025/12/18/pope-leo-appoints-ronald-hicks-archbishop-new-york-replacing-cardinal-timothy-dolan" target="_blank" >leader of the Archdiocese of New York</a> — one of the most prominent roles in the Catholic church. He was formally installed in February.</p>

entries.title: Bears predictions: Week 2 vs. Vikings
entries.summary: <p>The Sun-Times’ <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> experts make their picks for Sunday's home opener: </p><h3>Patrick Finley</h3><p><b>Bears, 28-24:</b> I'm more concerned about the Vikings defense giving up the third-fewest rushing yards in the NFL last week than I am their blitz scheme, which Caleb Williams traditionally handles with aplomb. When he was sacked 68 times in 2024, only five came from the Vikes. <b>Last week</b>: 0-1.</p><h3>Jason Lieser</h3><p><b>Bears, 34-29:</b> The Bears aren't going to rip up a Brian Flores defense like they did to the Panthers' last week, but they'll put up enough points to outrun their defensive troubles. <b>Last week:</b> 1-0.</p><h3>Scoop Jackson</h3><p><b>Bears, 36-30: </b>Flores’ defense does have the capability of slowing this Bears offense down. 400 yards of offense down from 552, 36 points down from 59. Yeah, that’s down. <b>Last week: </b>0-1.</p><h3>Steve Greenberg</h3><p><b>Bears, 30-24:</b> Eight touchdowns? Uh, no. Enough of them? Along with a few kicks to get the job done, yes. But Williams and the offense will be pressed hard to overcome a gung-ho pass rush. <b>Last week</b>: 1-0.</p><h3>Jeff Agrest</h3><p><b>Bears, 35-24:</b> Blitz, shmitz! Williams isn't afraid of the Vikings’ big, bad blitzes brought by Flores. And the Bears shouldn’t be afraid of the Vikings’ offense, outside of Justin Jefferson, of course. Happy home opener! <b>Last week: </b>0-1.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/10/bears-season-predictions-final-record-2026-ben-johnson-caleb-williams-nfl" >Bears season predictions: Where will they finish in 2026?</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Wheaton North's Adam Schilling makes plays on offense, defense one year after knee injury
entries.summary: <p>Adam Schilling could be forgiven for feeling a full circle moment this week.</p><p>It was this Friday last year, against the same opponent, that the Wheaton North tight end/linebacker’s season ended. On the last play of the game against St. Charles East, Schilling took a wrong step on a pass route. A Grade 2 PCL tear put Schilling in a knee brace for 2-3 months, and ended his season. His was one of a rash of injuries that sunk the Falcons.</p><p>Schilling, now a senior, is back. Wheaton North appears to be as well.</p><p>The Falcons, coming off back-to-back losing seasons, are 4-0. They are the lone unbeaten left in the DuKane Conference. This Friday they host 3-1 St. Charles East in a matchup of surprise teams.</p><p>“I have thought about it, what happened to me in this game last year,” Schilling said.</p><p>Wheaton North is swimming against a current in one of the state’s toughest leagues. Program numbers are not where they need to be. The Falcons do not have enough linemen in the junior and senior classes to play JV, the only school in the league not doing so. A lack of linemen depth predicated a switch to a 3-4 defense from its usual 40 front.</p><p>The Falcons do have skill.</p><p>Senior running back Mac Murray has rushed for 616 yards and nine touchdowns, and went over 200 yards in a win over Lake Park.</p><p>And Schilling, 6-5 and also a basketball player, has eight catches for 210 yards and four TDs, with 17 tackles and two tackles for loss at inside linebacker.</p><p>“Schilling is our best football player,” Wheaton North coach Joe Wardynski said. “He is a physical kid, smart, he has great hands. If we were throwing the ball more we’d be throwing to him a bunch. He has been a great blocker for us in the run game.</p><p>“He is very athletic for a big kid. He’s athletic, he can bend, he is explosive. We have not had very many better than him.”</p><p>Schilling was a tight end/receiver going back to freshman year. His wingspan helps in the passing game and shedding blocks and he can run past defenders.</p><p>He’s made strides as a blocker.</p><p>“I remember I had a meeting with our offensive coordinator end of sophomore year, and blocking was a big priority,” Schilling said. “They knew I could catch balls but my blocking was where I needed to improve. Got in the weight room, got stronger. I’ve continued to see growth with blocking, working on all different types of techniques.”</p><p>Schilling, who has moved from outside linebacker to inside, has a similar length and build to former Wheaton North star Ross Dansdill, now at Holy Cross, but Wardynski said Schilling’s more athletic.</p><p>“He’s 215 pounds, runs well and has no scholarship offers. It’s kind of mind boggling to me,” Wardynski said. “I am shocked that some of these D2 schools are not offering.”</p><p>Wheaton North, which broke into the Super 25 this week after beating St. Charles North, has work to do to continue its fast start.</p><p>The Falcons’ first four opponents currently hold a combined 4-12 record. They still have Batavia, Geneva and Wheaton-Warrenville South the last four weeks.</p><p>“We can’t be content,” Schilling said. “The teams we are going to face are increasingly difficult. We have to get better day in and day out.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.shawlocal.com/friday-night-drive/" target="_blank" >Read more high school football coverage on Friday Night Drive.</a></p>

entries.title: West Suburban, Weiss to be sold to Insight Health Systems
entries.summary: <p>West Suburban Medical Center and Weiss Memorial Hospital will be sold to Insight Health Systems, bringing a monthslong bitter legal fight over the hospitals to an end.</p><p>The hospitals’ landlord, Rathnakar Reddy Patlola, made a late-night deal Wednesday to buy Resilience Healthcare CEO Manoj Prasad's stake in the hospitals. Insight will then buy the hospitals from Patlola.</p><p>Representatives for Patlola and Prasad could not immediately be reached for comment.</p><p>In a statement, Insight President and CEO Atif Bawahab said the company would assess both hospitals to "determine the appropriate path forward," and that the agreement was the start of a "long, phased process."</p><p>"There are real hurdles ahead — restoring licenses and certifications, rebuilding systems and staffing, meeting regulatory requirements, and earning back the confidence of patients and providers — and none of that happens overnight," Bawahab said.</p><p>No specific dollar amounts were immediately made public. It was also not clear how — or if — the deal would reopen either hospital.</p><p>On Friday, Cook County Circuit Judge Patrick Stanton <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/09/11/west-suburban-weiss-memorial-hospitals-receivership-legal-battle" target="_blank" ><u>decided to put a receiver</u></a> in charge of the hospitals after presiding over months of bickering in his courtroom between the lawyers representing the business partners turned foes.</p><p>Stanton originally said a receiver would be announced Tuesday. Instead, on Tuesday and Wednesday, Stanton and lawyers met behind closed doors while interested parties and reporters waited for hours in his courtroom.</p><p>The legal battle centers around Prasad's decision to shut down West Suburban Medical Center in Oak Park in March. Patlola then sued him for control of the hospital and Weiss Memorial Hospital in the Uptown neighborhood, which closed in August 2025. Weiss also recently lost its state hospital license.</p><p>Patlola’s legal team <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/08/04/ownership-change-west-suburban-weiss-potential-settlement" target="_blank" ><u>had been pushing for months</u></a> to enforce a settlement agreement that includes selling the hospitals for $1 to Insight Health Systems. Prasad, who would have to step down as CEO and take on a temporary consulting position, had resisted that deal.</p><p>Insight runs Insight Hospital and Medical Center, formerly Mercy Hospital. The company bought the Bronzeville hospital on Chicago’s Near South Side for $1 in 2021, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/environment-public-health/2021/10/25/inside-the-fight-to-save-chicagos-historic-mercy-hospital" target="_blank" ><u>preventing it from closing</u></a>.</p><p>But Insight appears to have <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/08/08/insight-health-systems-west-suburban-medical-center-weiss-memorial-hospital" target="_blank" ><u>its own financial troubles</u></a>, raising questions about how it can afford to take on two more hospitals. Insight Hospital has consistently lost money since buying Mercy, WBEZ and the Chicago Sun-Times revealed last month. In 2024, the hospital lost nearly $30 million, the most recent records show.</p><p>That same year, Insight Hospital leaders told the state they faced “a financial emergency,” according to records obtained through a public records request.</p><p>Insight Hospital has received about $50 million in advances from the Illinois Department of Healthcare and Family Services to help keep the doors open since it bought Mercy. Last month, a healthcare and family services spokesperson said Insight had paid back just over $1 million so far, and that the department “has no plans to provide additional support at this time.”</p><p>Insight, West Suburban and Weiss are all safety-net hospitals, which are often the fabric of low-income and immigrant communities. They typically don’t make much money and struggle to make ends meet.</p>

entries.title: Chicago police timekeeper charged with sexually abusing 14-year-old girl he allegedly met on dating app
entries.summary: <p>A city staffer who works as a timekeeper for the Chicago Police Department was charged Thursday with sexually abusing a 14-year-old he met on a teen dating app, according to police and court records.</p><p>Oswaldo Lorenzana de La Rosa, 30, was arrested Tuesday in Albany Park following a brief foot pursuit, according to a police report and a police department spokesperson. He works as a police timekeeper for the Office of Public Safety Administration, earning a $61,548 annual salary, city records show.</p><p>On Aug. 19, the girl's mother went to the police department's Albany Park District and reported that Lorenzana de La Rosa had picked her daughter up from school every Thursday between April and July in order to have sexual relations at his Belmont Cragin home. He used the same Subaru Impreza for "every encounter," the police report states.</p><p>The girl told police she met Lorenzana de La Rosa on a dating app for teens and knew him as “Javier,'' according to the report. It says he offered her marijuana and alcohol, bought her clothing and flowers and gave her handwritten letters.</p><p>Lorenzana de La Rosa was charged with felony counts of criminal sexual assault, aggravated criminal sexual abuse, traveling to meet a minor, indecent solicitation of a child and grooming, court records show.</p><p>He's expected to appear at a detention hearing Thursday at the Leighton Criminal Courthouse.</p>
entries.author: Cindy Hernandez

entries.title: As everyday stint ends, ‘old soul’ Pedro Ramirez keeps impressing Cubs: ‘He can pretty much do everything’
entries.summary: <p>Pedro Ramirez did his job.</p><p>The 22-year-old rookie was thrust into everyday duty on the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ infield when shortstop Dansby Swanson went down with an oblique injury a month ago.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/16/chicago-cubs-dansby-swanson-rehab-return-friday-strained-left-oblique-reds-gavin-hollowell-riley-martin" >Swanson is due back Friday</a>, returning Ramirez to his reserve role with the Cubs fighting to secure a wild-card spot.</p><p>But Ramirez, as inexperienced as he was coming into the season, doesn’t appear to have been “thrust” into anything.</p><p>“Some people have a presence – I’ve called it ‘an old soul,’ at times – where you’re just comfortable with him immediately,” manager Craig Counsell said of Ramirez this week. “It’s not flashy, in any way, but you’re comfortable with him. He’s the kind of person that makes you trust him quickly.</p><p>“He’s also a talented baseball player. But you throw on that other stuff, and it’s a big reason why he’s a Major League Baseball player at such a young age. That’s how he carries himself.”</p><p>As important as Swanson is, particularly on defense, there didn’t seem to be much fretting when he went down. The Cubs had Gold Glove second baseman Nico Hoerner, who <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/04/cubs-nico-hoerner-dansby-swanson-shortstop-gold-glove-best-defense-in-baseball-oblique-injury" >slid over to his former stomping grounds at shortstop</a>.</p><p>But they also had Ramirez.</p><p>“Pedro is the kind of player, from early on in spring training, he impressed everyone with his demeanor,” Hoerner said Wednesday. “He’s a guy we all enjoy being around. He’s fun, has a good time with it, but he’s also very serious about his career. He’s got big aspirations for being a great player in this league.</p><p>“It could be a hard thing, learning to play at the big league level in the middle of a playoff chase and all that, and he’s balanced that really well.”</p><p>Like any player, Ramirez has gone through his ups and downs.</p><p>Though he homered off reigning Cy Young winner Paul Skenes on the most recent home stand, he’s in the middle of a slump, hitting .143 in his last 14 games, a stretch that’s dropped his OPS from .801 to .733. His OPS-plus of 100 makes his season output exactly league average.</p><p>But you wouldn’t know it the way the Cubs continue to rave about him.</p><p>“It’s impressive, because he’s the kind of player, he can pretty much do everything on the field,” Hoerner said. “He’s got real power that I think is going to show up even more so as he continues to play.</p><p>“It’s a really great sign that he can both be present and competing every day and helping us win while also continuing to develop and find the best version of himself.”</p><p>Regardless of recent numbers, that Ramirez, getting his first taste of the majors, has made himself a factor for a veteran team chasing a championship is no small thing.</p><p>During Swanson’s absence, Ramirez received regular playing time, something he wasn’t doing before, when he made an impact as a part-timer. This could go down as a valuable stretch.</p><p>“What any young player wants is consistent playing time. It’s the hardest thing to get, and you have to earn it,” Counsell said. “We’ve also gotten Pedro a number of at-bats that he can truly reflect on and improve on, too, a big enough sample where it’s fair to say, “What do we need to get better at?’</p><p>“Major league hitting, you just need the experience, you need the at-bats, you need to see the different pitch shapes, you need to see the greatness of some of these guys, the challenges: ‘How do they exploit you? What holes are they uncovering?’ And you can’t do that without consistent at-bats.</p><p>“Pedro’s gotten them.”</p><p>With Hoerner, Swanson and third baseman Alex Bregman are entrenched on the infield, what will Ramirez’s future role be?</p><p>Might he end up in the outfield? He has little experience, playing one inning in left field this season, with minimal time in the minors. But the Cubs could have holes to fill, with both left fielder Ian Happ and right fielder Seiya Suzuki slated to hit free agency.</p><p>But that’s to figure out later. Right now, it’s about what sort of contributions Ramirez can make to a team chasing a playoff spot – and a whole lot more – in September and October.</p><p>Not a bad opportunity for the 22-year-old with an old soul.</p>
